http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30116v1.title: Environment Duels: A Microcosm of LLM Co-Evolution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30116v1.abstract: Through a tangle of real-world interactions, from synthetic training pipelines to data shared on the open web, frontier LLMs absorb what their predecessors and competitors create. How well does each model play its role in this ecosystem, as a creator and as a solver? We introduce Environment Duels, a dynamic agentic benchmark that evaluates both capabilities on interactive environments. Each model writes environments, each with a privileged hint, aiming for tasks that capable solvers fail without the hint and pass with it. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29792v1.title: MAPS: Macro-Adaptive Parallel Reasoning for Regulating Search Momentum in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29792v1.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external knowledge. Recently, some RAG methods interleave reasoning and retrieval, enabling LLMs to progressively generate sub-queries and retrieve external knowledge. However, these methods may suffer from redundant or ineffective sub-queries and insufficiently diverse query exploration. Moreover, due to the tightly interleaved nature of reasoning and retrieval, it remains unclear how the evolving reasoning process influences query intent. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29870v1.title: PAUSE: Search-Free Steering of Coding Agents Before Their First Source-Code Edit
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29870v1.abstract: Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. Existing online steering methods review trajectories periodically or invoke an advisor when a monitor detects behavioral problems; frequent reviews are costly, and the absence of anomalous behavior does not mean that an agent is on the right track. We propose PAUSE, a framework for steering coding agents with a single planning intervention. Agents reach their first source-code edit at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, after exploration, bug reproduction, and testing.

http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30047v1.title: SWE-DIVE: Multi-Turn Coding Agent Evaluation with Dynamic User Simulation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30047v1.abstract: Coding agents are typically evaluated using one-shot, well-formulated prompts. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench use existing GitHub issues as input for a coding agent and evaluate whether the agent successfully solves the task. However, in real-world use cases, prompts are often not as well-formulated or structured as existing GitHub issues. Additionally, a coding agent session is not limited to a single prompt; it typically involves a multi-turn interaction in which the user iteratively adds new tasks and requirements that the agent must fulfill. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29812v1.title: Real PMIDs, Wrong Papers: Harness Design for Biomedical Claim-Verification Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29812v1.abstract: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30051v1.title: From Reasoning to Action: Benchmarking Frontier AI Models on LIBERO-10 Robot Manipulation Tasks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30051v1.abstract: Recent advances in frontier AI models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use, raising the possibility of using general-purpose AI models for robot manipulation without task-specific training. However, their manipulation capabilities have not been systematically evaluated on standardized robotics benchmarks. In this report, we present a unified closed-loop manipulation framework for evaluating frontier AI models on the LIBERO-10 benchmark. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30041v1.title: Robust Soft Skill Adaptation via Behavioral Localization in Tool-Using Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30041v1.abstract: Text skills can extend the capabilities of tool-using agents, but long skill descriptions increase computational costs. Soft prompts provide a compact alternative, yet learning from entire successful trajectories may also introduce unnecessary behavioral changes. We find that the useful effect of a text skill is highly concentrated in a small subset of trajectory positions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30014v1.title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30014v1.abstract: LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30072v1.title: Charts as Epistemic Actions for Experience-Driven Agentic Data Analysis
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30072v1.abstract: Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29822v1.title: UserSWE: Evaluating Coding Agents in Multi-Turn Conversations with Dynamic Users
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29822v1.abstract: As coding agents become more capable, developers increasingly use them to fix bugs through multi-turn interactions. Existing benchmarks do not adequately cover this scenario. Most present a complete issue report in a single turn without interaction. Their evaluation can produce both false positives and false negatives, accepting incorrect patches or rejecting correct ones. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29932v1.title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29932v1.abstract: Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29749v1.title: Metamodel-Guided LLM Decoding for Consistent DSL Generation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29749v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate software engineering artifacts written in domain-specific languages (DSLs). Correct DSL instances usually must comply with not only the concrete syntax but also the abstract syntax defined by a metamodel augmented with semantic well-formedness constraints. Existing constrained decoding approaches typically guarantee compliance only with concrete syntax or with a limited set of semantic constraints expressed over the generated text, making metamodel-level constraint consistency difficult to enforce during generation. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30042v1.title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30042v1.abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29823v1.title: MemoryTax: The Bitter Lesson of Agent Memory
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29823v1.abstract: Agent memory systems such as Mem0 and Zep decide what to keep before any question arrives; coding agents keep the raw history and let the model search it with its own tools. We ask whether designed memory still helps once the model is strong enough to search for itself. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30103v1.title: Did the Problem Actually Get Harder? Testing LLMs on Paired P and NP-Complete Problems Hardened by Adversarial Multi-Agent Rewriting
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30103v1.abstract: Many NP-complete (NPC) problems have a polynomial-time (P) twin that differs in a single structural detail, such as 3- versus 2-colouring a graph. A model that reasons rather than recalls should notice which side of this boundary a problem falls on, yet existing benchmarks either fix the wording of each task or ignore its complexity class, so they cannot separate the two. We introduce P2NPCBench, a benchmark of 12 problem families in which every NPC problem is paired with a P twin posed over the same surface. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31080v1.title: nnInteractive Agent: General-Purpose AI Agents as 3D Image Annotators
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31080v1.abstract: Interactive 3D segmentation models such as nnInteractive turn a few spatial prompts (points, scribbles, boxes) into accurate volumetric masks, but a human still does the annotation work: finding each structure, placing prompts, checking the result and correcting it. General-purpose AI agents can now interpret images, call tools and write code. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30284v1.abstract: Coding agents spend substantial computation generating actions and processing long interaction histories. Poor action choices can steer agents into low-value states, wasting computation and increasing API costs. Sampling and verifying alternative actions can improve the agent's decisions, but applying this procedure at every step adds substantial overhead. We introduce SWE-Verifier, a lightweight generative model that selectively triggers candidate sampling and verification. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30557v1.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30557v1.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30917v1.title: Harnessing Language Models as Optimization Modeling Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30917v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language optimization problems into solver programs, but reliably producing correct formulations and implementations remains challenging. Existing approaches improve optimization modeling through agentic workflows or task-specific post-training. This raises a practical question: can a lightweight harness using a single model role achieve competitive performance without additional training? http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31158v1.title: Beyond Watching and Searching: Benchmarking Agents for Video-centered Deep Research Reports
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31158v1.abstract: Deep research agents synthesize open-web evidence into long reports, but current benchmarks do not evaluate research centered on a source video. We introduce Video-Centered Deep Research Report Generation. Given a video and user request, an agent identifies research questions, retrieves external multimodal evidence, and produces an interactive report linked to relevant video moments. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30524v1.title: LLM2Cert: LLM Synthesis of Certificates with SMT/Lean Verification
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30524v1.abstract: Lyapunov functions and barrier certificates give state-space guarantees of stability and safety, but synthesizing and verifying them---especially for nonlinear, high-dimensional systems---remains an open challenge. Existing pipelines verify candidates with numerical solvers (sum-of-squares programs), interval methods, or satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers, which often require relaxations, are conservative, or scale poorly with model dimension and nonlinearity. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30573v1.title: Diagnosing Personalization Failures in Mobile GUI Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30573v1.abstract: Unlike conventional GUI agents, personalized GUI agents require user preferences to guide sequential execution over changing GUI states. This raises two challenges: determining HOW each preference should alter execution strategy and WHEN it should take effect along the interaction trajectory. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate overall task success, offering limited insight into these questions. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30355v1.title: CiteAnchor: Source-Aware Grounding for Hallucinated Citation Detection and Resolution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30355v1.abstract: Hallucinated citations make it harder to trace sources and verify the evidence behind scientific claims. Detecting them is difficult because bibliographic records can be incomplete or differ across source types and publication versions. A plausible match alone neither validates the citation nor establishes its underlying source. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31120v1.title: SetCommit: Coordinated Token Commitments for Few-Step Diffusion Language Model Decoding
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31120v1.abstract: Diffusion language models generate multiple token positions in parallel, but few-step decoding makes parallel commitment difficult: tokens that appear reliable individually may be jointly inconsistent, while premature commitments can prevent later context-dependent refinement. In this paper, we introduce SetCommit, a training-free method for coordinated parallel token commitment. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30946v1.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate UML class diagrams from natural language requirements, but hallucinations may compromise the correctness and completeness of the resulting diagrams. Existing evaluations mostly assess the final diagram, without examining the intermediate traces of reasoning-capable LLMs, which can reveal where these hallucinations arise. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30412v1.abstract: LLM-based chat agents are increasingly used for complex, multi-turn, multilingual medical triage in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), yet evaluation methods focus on single-turn, English-only benchmarks that primarily test the chatbots' knowledge. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30843v1.abstract: We introduce Lean Finder V2, a semantic search framework for Mathlib that disambiguates user queries through complementary model-level adversarial training and input-level query rewriting. Human mathematicians and coding agents rarely search Mathlib by providing detailed context. In practice, they query short properties, notation, aliases, or hypotheses, leaving much of the intended mathematics implicit. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.30491v1.abstract: LLM agents are often evaluated by reducing execution traces to labels such as final-answer correctness, tool verification, and fault propagation. These labels are measurements produced by parsers, behavioral detectors, and harness rules, and they may not fully capture what the trace shows. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31511v1.title: DuoCook: An Overcooked-Inspired Benchmark for Visual Planning and Coordination
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31511v1.abstract: Coordinating two players in a cooking task requires a vision-language agent to track changing scene states, sequence recipe steps, and allocate shared resources under a time budget. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31148v1.title: Prompt Sensitivity in Tool-Augmented Model Comparisons
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31148v1.abstract: Language models are compared on question-answering benchmarks that pose each question in one wording, and a reworded question can change which of two models scores higher. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32725v1.abstract: The rapid expansion of scientific literature far outpaces the speed of manual curation, creating a fundamental bottleneck in extracting structured knowledge from scientific texts. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32181v1.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions under incomplete information, where deciding what to look up and when to stop matters as much as the final answer. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32441v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents' strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31854v1.abstract: Greenfield software development in freelance settings requires coding agents to turn incomplete client requests into working software. This makes requirement clarification essential, yet clients may be unable to provide continuous feedback over long development cycles, and receiving their answers does not guarantee correct understanding of complex requirements. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32305v1.title: DMAIC-Bench: From Self-Reflection to Self-Restraint for Agents in Multi-Stage Analytical Tasks
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32305v1.abstract: Multi-stage analytical tasks require LLM agents to use intermediate evidence to decide whether to continue, redirect or stop. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32295v1.abstract: Lifelong LLM agents must learn from an expanding history of interactions while making each decision within a bounded context window. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32813v1.abstract: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31882v1.title: TACS-RF: Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave Modules
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31882v1.abstract: We present the framework of TACS-RF - a Tool-driven Agentic Circuit Synthesis of RF and mmWave modules. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32110v1.abstract: Agents and verifiers often rely on the text a tool prints, and that text can misrepresent what the tool actually did, even when the tool's computation is correct. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31809v1.abstract: A bug report describes what went wrong, but rarely where the code should change. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32195v1.abstract: Scientific discovery requires identifying the scientific principles underlying observed phenomena to guide further investigation. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33274v1.title: FlexA-Mem: Budget-Adaptive Agentic Memory for LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33274v1.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents work in scenarios with very different memory needs. A question about past conversations needs the exact facts it names, while a multi-step task needs a trace of the steps already taken together with details that the next step cannot name. Existing memories are each designed and tested for one kind of scenario. Retrieval memories such as A-Mem miss steps that the current query does not express, summaries drop exact strings, and pairing the two fixes the split of the budget in advance. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34167v1.title: Task Success Is Not Enough: Side-effect-Aware Evaluation of Tool-Using Language Model Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34167v1.abstract: Tool-using language model agents are usually evaluated by whether they finish the user's task. That metric misses a common failure: an agent can complete the requested work while also taking an unauthorized side-effecting action, such as writing to the wrong object, expanding the scope of the request, or contacting an unintended recipient. We call this failure mode collateral damage (CD). We introduce SABench (Side-effect-Aware Benchmark), a benchmark of 201 email, calendar, and ticket tasks. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37201v1.title: Does Your Generalist Skill Optimizer Really Incentivize Agentic Tasks? Rethinking Skill Optimization via Bipartite Attribution
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37201v1.abstract: Skill optimizers adapt an agent to long-horizon tasks, such as repairing a terminal environment, by rewriting its skill, a natural-language procedure in its context, and keeping the edits that raise success on a small dev set. On such tasks success is noisy, so a gain on a small dev set does not show that an edit helps, and a success score does not show what the edit costs. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37224v1.title: Spine: Compiling Subtask Trees into Structured Context for Long-Horizon Coding Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37224v1.abstract: Long-horizon coding tasks contain nested subtasks. Typically, agents record interactions sequentially into a growing history, causing context inflation and performance degradation. Compressing or trimming the history without explicit subtask boundaries can discard information needed by unfinished subtasks. Conversely, recursive subagent delegation isolates completed subtasks through child agents by assigning every subtask boundary to delegation, which conflates subtask granularity with executing agent choice, adding execution and coordination overhead. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33929v1.title: WebViSE: Scaling Visual Design Intelligence from the Open Web for LLM Website Generation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33929v1.abstract: Large language models have made remarkable strides in website development, enabling complete and interactive web experiences to be built from natural-language instructions with far less effort. Yet, non-expert users often struggle to articulate sophisticated visual and interaction designs in natural language. Meanwhile, the open web already contains a vast reservoir of such design knowledge, embodied in mature website implementations. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35333v1.title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35333v1.abstract: Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34425v1.title: CTXAgent - Self-Controlled Context Management of LLM Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.34425v1.abstract: Agent harnesses keep long sessions inside the context window by compacting the history when a token threshold is crossed. We study an alternative in which the model manages its own context: it decides when to compact, what to keep and what to write as the hand-off, given two tools and one paragraph of guidance. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36108v1.title: Log-To-Leak: Prompt Injection Attacks on Tool-Using LLM Agents via the Model Context Protocol
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36108v1.abstract: LLM agents increasingly access external tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), but the natural-language metadata used to describe those tools creates a prompt-injection surface. Within this established tool-poisoning surface, we study Log-To-Leak, an additive post-hoc logging attack that induces a separate attacker-controlled call after the final legitimate call. Its payload targets the user query, MCP server name, server response, and agent response. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35426v1.title: Intent-Preserving Adversarial User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agent Evaluation
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35426v1.abstract: Multi-turn agents are commonly evaluated with LLM-based simulated users, which can be overly cooperative and can therefore overestimate an agent's performance. We here introduce StressSim, an intent-preserving adversarial user simulator framework for stress-testing agents with challenging yet valid user interactions. StressSim optimises the simulator's high-level adversarial plan for each task instance. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33861v1.title: ReGE: Stronger Agents through Experience Synthesis
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33861v1.abstract: Repeated attempts at interactive tasks uncover facts, useful operations, and failures that can inform subsequent execution. We introduce ReGE, a framework for turning this recorded experience into guidance for a fresh attempt. Its main implementation, ReGE-Syn, uses a single coach call to jointly synthesize bounded execution records and available artifacts into self-contained guidance, connecting task-specific findings with proposed actions and relevant pitfalls. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.35616v1.abstract: Skills provide agents with reusable experience to guide future decisions without modifying the underlying model. However, coding trajectories are often entangled with task- and repository-specific contexts, making it challenging to distill procedural skills that generalize across diverse coding environments. To address this challenge, we present Hierarchical Skill Evolution (HSE), which progressively distills procedural knowledge from coding trajectories through hierarchical evidence aggregation. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1.title: Remembering Is Not Enough: Refining Memories and Learning When to Use Them in Multi-Agent Systems
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36652v1.abstract: Memory helps LLM-based multi-agent systems reuse experience, but stored advice can be flawed or applied in the wrong situation. Team-level success or failure alone cannot reliably show whether a memory needs correction or should not have been used. We propose DiscernMem, a training-free framework that improves both memory quality and memory use. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37651v1.title: GEPA-Curator: Curated Learning for Self Improving Agents
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.37651v1.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in multi-turn agentic workloads that require sustained interaction with complex environments. Existing reflective prompt optimizers such as GEPA learn from failed rollouts, but agentic failures can also come from prompt weaknesses, harness limitations, stochastic execution, or noisy judges. We argue that such failures may not provide useful learning signal, and may even be harmful; and thus it is essential to curate which tasks are provided to the prompt optimizer for better performance. http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33245v1.title: AdaPRA: Process Reward Agents with Adaptive Rubrics for Data Science
http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.33245v1.abstract: Data science agents can automate end-to-end machine learning workflows, yet they remain far from competitive on human leaderboards. Agents make process errors such as insufficient exploration, unsound validation, coding bugs, and poor use of a fixed budget (re-running the same exploratory data analysis and baseline models in every attempt).
